verdicts.quote: The spreadsheet step is automatically triggered when the nurse saves the ward note in the system — no extra action needed.

The ward manager gets an email alert every morning at 7:30 a.m. with a list of patients who have new notes since the previous day, including a link to view the note and download the updated spreadsheet.
If a nurse forgets to enter a note, the system sends a reminder to them and their team leader at 10 a.m. the next day.
The spreadsheet step is automatically triggered when the nurse saves the ward note in the system — no extra action needed.
If a nurse enters a note after 8 a.m., the spreadsheet still gets updated, but the quality team logs it as a delay.
If a note isn’t entered by 10 a.m. the next day, it stays in the system as a pending task for the nurse, but the team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse’s name and patient full name.
The finance supervisor also uses it once a month to match nurse hours with documented patient interactions.
the same note must appear in ShareSheet by 8 a.m. the next day.
the team leader's 10:15 a.m. alert includes the nurse's name, the missing patient, and the time, and FR-12 gets updated to match.
We can add the quality team’s weekly logging in version two, as long as the core workflow works and the nurses can use it without extra steps.
If it doesn’t, the system must show a clear error message than silently fail. And if it does fail, the nurse must know exactly what to do — like retry or contact IT.

when the first note is saved and ShareSheet is unreachable, the nurse should see a clear message on screen... The note stays in the system on their device, and the system automatically retries every 5 minutes for up to 30 minutes.

the system must also prevent nurses from editing a note after 48 hours — once it’s been synced, it’s final, unless a supervisor approves a correction. ... The system should flag any edit after 48 hours and send it to the team leader for review.

No direct quote about team leader dashboard flags before 8 a.m., but participant said: 'If there had been a simple alert — like a red flag in the team leader’s daily dashboard showing “1 note pending by 8 a.m.” — they could have acted at 7:45 a.m.'

When the ward manager opens the system each morning, the first thing they see is a summary dashboard with three key items: the number of notes entered so far today, how many are overdue (more than 10 a.m.), and a list of nurses who haven’t entered a note yet.
The manager then sends a quick message through the system to the nurse — no phone calls needed — saying “Hi, just checking in on your notes for Mr. Smith. Thanks!”
If a nurse has missed two notes in a row, the manager gets a yellow alert and can schedule a quick 5-minute huddle to check in.
If they’re new to the system, they get a short video pop-up the first time, but only once.
the team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse’s name and patient full name. The alert includes a direct link to the note entry page.
If a note is missing by 9:30 a.m., the system escalates it to the ward manager automatically.
